newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK consumer stocks return to favour.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK consumer stocks return to favour.

text.p: Shares in Britain's consumer-oriented companies continued to storm ahead on Friday as investors piled into a sector viewed by analysts as the current darling of the stockmarket.

The strong bull run in the sector, which kicked off in earnest on Wednesday, stems from a range of factors, said analysts, including the strength of sterling, consumer demand, the budget and recent underperformance in the sector relative to the all share index.
Full year results from Dixons Group Plc, posted on Wednesday, showed the strength of high street sales, pushing shares in the electrical retailer to a year high.
"People have looked at the retailers first and are now looking for the next sector to benefit from this improved outlook for consumers," said Nick Lyall, an analyst at SocGen.

Many stockbrokers have responded by hurriedly issuing their clients with "buy" recommendations on pub companies and leisure groups. On Friday shares in Britain's largest brewer Scottish and Newcastle Plc, owners of Center Parcs holiday resorts, punched through its record high, rising 37p to 747-1/2p at 1200 GMT.

Shares in Whitbread Plc, which owns 16 Marriott hotels in Britain as well as French bistro style Cafe Rouge and Cafe Dome restaurants, also set a record high of 834p, up 40 pence by 1200 GMT. Bass Plc shares were 21p higher at 829p.

The argument goes that sterling's strength on the foreign exchange markets has depressed the earnings of exporters but increased the attraction of companies whose income is derived from the domestic economy.

Brokers also argue that the climate for consumer spending on low ticket items like eating out or a weekend break looks very rosy. Britain's consumers, currently flush with cash generated by huge building society windfalls, are tending to spend on small ticket items rather than on a car or house, analysts said.
"With all the worries about the currency going strong you have got to go for domestics," said Ron Littleboy, an analyst at Nomura.

"I think the stocks compared to other sectors look good value. The thoughts about higher interest rates might stop people from going out buying houses and cars and higher ticket items but that means people have plenty of money for lower ticket items," he added.

A 1/4 point increase in interest rates to 6.75 percent, announced by the Bank of England on Thursday, has done little to quell that demand, they said, while Chancellor Gordon Brown's budget on May 4 has failed to hold down consumers' appetites on the high street.
Brown forecast consumer spending would rise by 4.5 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 1998.
"I'm a little bit surprised in a way that we did not see a rally more immediately after the budget," said Eric Frankis, an analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
The introduction of a minimum wage, a manifesto pledge of the ruling Labour Party, is also likely to favour pub companies as the lower waged tend to drink more beer, said analysts.
